segments.script: A 'living' was a church post with income controlled by a patron. Readers learn alongside Elizabeth that a confident story is not proof—central to the theme of prejudice. Characterization: Wickham tells Elizabeth that Darcy cheated him of a promised living; he says he will never expose Darcy, then does exactly that. Irony: Wickham claims discretion while gossiping to a near stranger. Watch for rank and condescension: Rank is displayed and enforced, above all at Rosings by Lady Catherine; Elizabeth refuses to be cowed. In this chapter: “have supposed himself in the small summer breakfast parlour at Rosings; a comparison that did not at first convey much gratification; but” (Chapter XVI, paragraph 2).

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “I have no right to give my opinion” slowly and put it in my own words: Wickham tells Elizabeth he has no right to give an opinion of Darcy, since he has known him too long to be impartial. Next, craft. I notice he pretends modesty and fairness while preparing to accuse Darcy. The strongest word is “right”: it shows him claiming a fairness he does not actually practice. Then, effect. Why does Wickham claim he cannot judge Darcy fairly? My answer: Wickham's false modesty makes his later accusations seem believable; Elizabeth trusts him because he flatters her own dislike of Darcy.
